Acinetobacter baumannii: A hospital-associated pathogen that causes ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream and wound infections, especially in intensive care. Resistance islands and insertion sequences help it acquire multidrug resistance, including carbapenem resistance, and adapt to hospital environments.
Campylobacter coli: Common in pigs and other livestock, this bacterium is the second most frequent cause of human campylobacteriosis after C. jejuni. It causes acute gastroenteritis. Frequent recombination within and between Campylobacter species, especially with C. jejuni, complicates phylogenetic analysis.
Campylobacter jejuni: A leading cause of foodborne gastroenteritis, often acquired from undercooked poultry, unpasteurised milk or contaminated water. Its small, AT-rich genome contains phase-variable loci. Natural uptake of DNA and frequent recombination add to the diversity seen between strains.
Enterobacter cloacae: Found in soil, water and the human gut, this opportunistic pathogen causes hospital-acquired bloodstream, respiratory, urinary and wound infections. It belongs to the E. cloacae complex and carries an inducible AmpC beta-lactamase; mobile elements can add further resistance genes.
Enterococcus faecium: A gut bacterium that has become a major cause of hospital-acquired infection, including bacteraemia, endocarditis and urinary tract infection. Vancomycin-resistant strains are a particular concern. Hospital-adapted lineages carry accessory genes linked to resistance and virulence.
Escherichia coli: Usually a harmless gut commensal, this bacterium also has pathogenic variants that cause urinary tract infections, bacteraemia, neonatal meningitis and diarrhoeal disease. Its open pangenome is shaped by plasmids, phages and horizontal gene transfer, making it a critical sentinel for antimicrobial resistance surveillance.
Haemophilus influenzae: A resident of the human respiratory tract that can cause invasive disease and common airway infections. Vaccination greatly reduced meningitis caused by encapsulated type b strains; non-typeable strains still cause otitis media, sinusitis and pneumonia. Its small genome readily takes up new DNA.
Klebsiella aerogenes: Formerly known as Enterobacter aerogenes, this bacterium occurs in the environment and human gut. It causes hospital-acquired pneumonia, urinary and bloodstream infections. An inducible AmpC beta-lactamase and acquired resistance genes can complicate treatment and contribute to outbreaks.
Klebsiella africana: First described from clinical isolates in Africa, this close relative of K. pneumoniae has also been recovered from human infections. Its clinical significance is still being defined. Core-genome relationships and accessory genes distinguish it from other members of the K. pneumoniae complex.
Klebsiella grimontii: A member of the K. oxytoca species complex found in clinical, environmental and food samples. Some isolates produce tilivalline, a cytotoxin linked to antibiotic-associated haemorrhagic colitis. Genomic methods distinguish it from closely related species in the complex.
Klebsiella huaxiensis: First isolated from clinical specimens in China, this member of the K. pneumoniae complex can be mistaken for K. pneumoniae by routine biochemical tests. Genome analysis places it in a distinct lineage; some isolates carry antimicrobial resistance genes of clinical concern.
Klebsiella michiganensis: A member of the K. oxytoca complex found in clinical, environmental and food samples. It can cause opportunistic infections, including bacteraemia and urinary tract infection. Some strains carry cytotoxin genes; others have acquired extended-spectrum beta-lactamase or carbapenemase genes.
Klebsiella oxytoca: Found in the gut, food and environment, this species causes urinary and bloodstream infections. Tilivalline-producing strains are linked to antibiotic-associated haemorrhagic colitis. Its chromosomal OXY beta-lactamase confers intrinsic resistance to amino- and carboxy-penicillins.
Klebsiella pasteurii: A recently delineated member of the K. oxytoca complex recovered from clinical and environmental sources. Routine phenotypic tests can misidentify it as K. oxytoca. Genome analysis separates the species, and some strains carry cytotoxin or antimicrobial resistance genes.
Klebsiella pneumoniae: An encapsulated opportunistic pathogen causing pneumonia, urinary tract and bloodstream infections, liver abscesses and neonatal sepsis. Hypervirulent strains can also cause severe community-acquired disease. Carbapenemase-producing lineages spread through plasmid-mediated gene transfer and diverse capsule types.
Klebsiella quasipneumoniae: A close relative of K. pneumoniae with two recognised subspecies, recovered from blood, urine and respiratory specimens. It can carry extended-spectrum beta-lactamase and carbapenemase genes, although multidrug resistance and hypervirulence are reported less often than in K. pneumoniae.
Klebsiella quasivariicola: A member of the K. pneumoniae complex closely related to K. variicola. Isolates come from both clinical and environmental sources and are often misclassified by phenotypic tests. Whole-genome sequencing separates the species and can reveal acquired resistance genes.
Klebsiella spallanzanii: A recently described member of the K. oxytoca complex first identified in clinical specimens. Phenotypic tests struggle to separate it from related species; core-genome analysis resolves it as a distinct lineage. Some isolates carry resistance and virulence-associated genes.
Klebsiella variicola: First described as a nitrogen-fixing plant endophyte, this relative of K. pneumoniae also causes bloodstream and urinary infections and neonatal sepsis. Routine tests can misidentify it as K. pneumoniae. Some strains acquire carbapenemase or hypervirulence plasmids.
Listeria monocytogenes: The cause of listeriosis, a serious foodborne infection affecting pregnant people, newborns, older adults and those with weakened immunity. It persists in food-processing environments because it tolerates cold, salt and low pH. Its genome encodes invasion and intracellular-survival factors.
Mycobacterium abscessus: A rapidly growing non-tuberculous mycobacterium that causes chronic lung infection in people with cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis, and skin or soft-tissue infection after injury or surgery. Intrinsic drug resistance and an inducible erm(41) gene complicate macrolide treatment.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis: The bacterium that causes tuberculosis spreads through respiratory aerosols and can persist as latent infection before reactivation. Its genome is relatively conserved, with little horizontal gene transfer. A GC-rich sequence and extensive lipid-metabolism genes underpin its distinctive cell wall.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae: The cause of gonorrhoea infects urogenital, rectal and pharyngeal mucosa. Untreated infection can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility or dissemination. Its naturally transformable genome supports antigenic variation and the continuing acquisition of antibiotic resistance.
Neisseria meningitidis: Often carried without symptoms in the nasopharynx, this bacterium can cause meningitis and rapidly progressing septicaemia. Its naturally transformable genome recombines frequently. Of its 13 capsular serogroups, A, B, C, W, X and Y account for most invasive disease.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Common in water and other moist environments, this opportunistic pathogen causes chronic lung infection in cystic fibrosis, ventilator-associated pneumonia and burn-wound infection. Its large genome encodes biofilm formation, secretion systems and efflux pumps that contribute to persistence and drug resistance.
Renibacterium salmoninarum: The cause of bacterial kidney disease in salmonid fish, a chronic systemic infection of concern to aquaculture. This slow-growing bacterium has a reduced genome with many insertion sequences, consistent with its intracellular lifestyle and limited metabolic independence.
Salmonella enterica: More than 2,600 serovars belong to this species, causing illness from self-limiting gastroenteritis to typhoid fever. Pathogenicity islands, prophages and fimbrial genes shape host adaptation, while a large, dynamic pangenome reflects the genetic diversity behind different host ranges and disease patterns.
Staphylococcus aureus: Often carried on the skin or in the nose, this bacterium can cause skin infection, food poisoning, endocarditis and sepsis. Methicillin-resistant strains remain a major clinical concern. Mobile genetic elements carry toxins, immune-evasion factors and antimicrobial resistance genes.
Stenotrophomonas maltophilia: An environmental bacterium that causes pneumonia, bloodstream and catheter-related infections, particularly in hospitalised or immunocompromised people. It is intrinsically resistant to many broad-spectrum antibiotics, including carbapenems, and contains genetically diverse lineages.
Streptococcus equi: Subspecies equi causes strangles, a contagious upper-respiratory disease of horses marked by swollen, abscessed lymph nodes. It evolved from the more diverse subspecies zooepidemicus through genome reduction and acquisition of virulence factors including SeM and SePE.
Streptococcus pneumoniae: Commonly carried in the nasopharynx, this bacterium causes pneumonia, meningitis, ear infection and sepsis. Its capsule defines more than 100 serotypes. Frequent recombination allows capsule switching and the acquisition of antibiotic resistance, complicating vaccine control.
Vibrio cholerae: Toxigenic O1 and O139 strains cause cholera by producing cholera toxin and the toxin-coregulated pilus; other strains occur in estuarine waters without causing epidemic disease. Its two-chromosome genome contains mobile elements and genomic islands associated with new pandemic lineages.
